newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin sees charter with Belarus signed on May 23.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin sees charter with Belarus signed on May 23.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin hopes to meet Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko on May 23 to sign a charter on forming a union between their two Slav former Soviet republics, a Kremlin spokesman said on Wednesday.

Yeltsin's press secretary, Sergei Yastrzhembsky, said the Kremlin leader had told Deputy Prime Minister Valery Serov to concentrate all his efforts on polishing the text of the charter in time to meet the deadline.
"By May 15 the final version of the charter should be presented to the presidents of both countries so that they can sign it by May 23," Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing.
Opinion polls in Russia and Belarus have shown that the majority of people in both countries back the idea of closer integration and even a merger.
But the union has met vociferous opposition from some circles in Russia and Belarus.

Belarus nationalists, who do not trust promises by Yeltsin and Lukashenko that the deal will not affect the sovereignty of either state, accuse Russia of imperialistic plans and see the union as a threat to the independence Minsk won in late 1991.

Russian liberals, who generally welcome closer integration with Belarus, have warned Yeltsin against striking a deal with the hardline Lukashenko, whose authoritarian rule and crackdown on civil rights have been criticised abroad.

The liberals also say a union with Belarus, where economic reforms are still at an embryonic stage, could slow down Russia's transition to a full market economy and turn out to be an unbearable financial burden for Moscow.
Their concerns led to a union treaty signed by Yeltsin and Lukashenko on April 2 being watered down.
Details of the union were sliced out and contained in the separate charter, which the two presidents initialled but, at Russia's insistence, delayed signing to allow public debate.

The Russia-Belarus union has also caused worries among Moscow and Minsk's partners in the Commonwealth of Independent States who say it could blow apart the wider 12-member grouping of former Soviet republics.
The latest versions of the documents provide for a loose union with little practical power delegated to it. Both Russia and Belarus would remain sovereign states.
